01The catalogue

A lane cannot sell anything until it knows what the shop stocks. The item master is a CSV, because that is what a distributor sends and what a shopkeeper can edit.

Adding items to the template

Open catalog_template.csv, replace the sample rows with the shop's own, and import it. Columns may be in any order and any case. The first nine are required; the last two are optional and may be left out of the file entirely.

ColumnRequiredWhat it is
skuyesYour own item code. Unique, case-insensitive.
barcodecolumn onlyBlank for loose goods. Unique where present.
nameyesWhat prints on the receipt and what the cashier searches.
hsn_codeyesRequired on a GST invoice for every line.
unityesPcs or Kg. L and M also accepted.
mrpyesPrinted maximum retail price.
selling_priceyesWhat you charge. May not exceed mrp.
gst_rateyesOne of 0, 5, 12, 18, 28. A trailing % is fine.
is_weighedyesMust agree with unit.
categorynoDepartment — Staples, Dairy, Household. Free text.
cost_pricenoWhat you pay for one. Between 0 and selling_price.
 
sku,barcode,name,hsn_code,unit,mrp,selling_price,gst_rate,is_weighed,category,cost_price
DAL001,8901234567890,Toor Dal 1kg,0713,Pcs,189.00,189.00,5,false,Staples,162.00
SUG001,,Sugar Loose,1701,Kg,45.00,45.00,5,true,Staples,41.50
ATT001,8901234567937,Wheat Atta Loose,1101,Kg,42.00,42.00,0,true,Staples,

That last row leaves cost_price blank on purpose. A blank means you have not said, which is a different thing from zero and is treated differently everywhere it matters.

Loading it

pos import-items --file catalogue.csv --dry-run
pos import-items --file catalogue.csv
pos import-items --file catalogue.csv --update   # a price revision
All or nothing

If anything is wrong, nothing is written and the catalogue is exactly as it was — and every problem in the file is reported at once, with line numbers. A shopkeeper fixing a spreadsheet wants the whole list, not the first line that failed.

What it refuses

  • A gst_rate outside the five slabs. Almost always a typo, and a typo here misprices every sale of that item until somebody notices.
  • A selling_price above mrp.
  • A cost_price above selling_price, or negative.
  • A barcode whose check digit does not add up — which would otherwise match a completely different product. Applies to 8, 12 and 13-digit codes; internal codes pass through.
  • The same SKU or barcode twice, or a barcode already belonging to another item.
  • unit and is_weighed disagreeing. One of them is wrong and there is no way to tell which.

Verified by ItemImportTests, CategoryAndCostTests · 15 checks on the two optional columns alone

02Ringing up a sale

There is no mouse in any of this. Every action is a keystroke, so the till can be worked with one hand on the scanner and one on the keyboard.

Items with a barcode are simply scanned — the till recognises a scanner by how fast the keystrokes arrive, so nothing needs pressing. Items without one are found by typing part of the name or the SKU.

KeyDoes
just scanAdds the item
F2Search by name or SKU
F3Type an exact quantity — this is how weights are entered
F4Discount the selected line
+ -Step the quantity
DeleteRemove the line
F5 / F6Park a bill / bring it back
F7Attach a customer by mobile
F12Take payment
Ctrl+USay who is on the till

Parked bills survive a restart and do not take an invoice number while they wait — so a bill that never gets settled leaves no hole in a run that has to be unbroken.

Verified by KeyboardOnlyFlowTests, InvoiceEngineTests, HeldBillPersistenceTests, LookupLatencyTests

03Taking payment

One key, then as many tenders as the customer wants to use.

Why points do not change the tax

Loyalty points are a way of paying, not a discount. They reduce what the customer hands over and leave every line's price, taxable value and GST untouched — so the same basket produces the same invoice whether it was paid in cash or partly in points. That is asserted directly, by pricing the same bill both ways and comparing.

Once the bill is fully paid, the invoice is written to disk first, and only then does anything print or the drawer open. A printer out of paper or a drawer that will not budge is reported on screen and never costs the sale.

Verified by TenderBasketTests, TenderFlowTests, LoyaltyEngineTests, CheckoutTests

04Receipts

Tamil or English, on any thermal printer, with the header a grocery bill in India is expected to carry.

Why Tamil is drawn, not typed

No thermal printer has a Tamil font, and none could: a syllable is assembled from several code points and reordered — the vowel sign in கெ is stored after the consonant and drawn before it. Nothing that maps bytes to glyphs one at a time can render that.

So the operating system's font engine draws those lines and they go down the wire as a raster image, sidestepping the printer's fonts entirely. Only the lines that need it — English still goes as characters, which is sharper, faster and a fraction of the data. It is also why the Tamil on a real shop bill looks like a different typeface from the English beside it.

Header fields

Store name, two address lines, GSTIN, FSSAI No and Customer Care — all from settings.json, all optional except the name.

A file saved in the wrong encoding

If settings.json is saved in the machine's ANSI encoding instead of UTF-8, a Tamil shop name becomes à®°à®µà®¿ and that is what prints on every bill. The mangled text is valid JSON and valid UTF-8, so nothing downstream can tell. The lane now refuses to start on it and says what the text was meant to be, and the templates ship with a byte-order mark so it cannot happen in the first place.

Verified by ReceiptTests, TamilReceiptTests, RasterLayoutTests, RasterImageTests, TamilRasterizationTests, TextEncodingCheckTests

05Snapshots

What a bill records is what was true when it was rung up — not what the catalogue says today.

Every invoice line carries its own copy of the item's name, HSN code, barcode, unit, MRP, unit price, GST rate, department and cost price, along with the tax that was actually charged. None of it is looked up from the catalogue when the bill is read back.

Why it matters

A shop renames items, moves them between departments, renegotiates what it pays, and revises prices. If a report joined back to the catalogue, every one of those changes would silently restate figures somebody has already acted on — last quarter's margin would move because a supplier's price moved this morning.

The consequence is worth stating plainly, and the dashboard states it on its own face: adding category and cost_price to a catalogue fills the charts in from that day forward, not backwards. Nobody knew an item's cost last March, and the software will not pretend it did.

Parked bills follow the same rule. A bill held before a price revision and settled after it keeps what it was parked with.

Verified by CategoryAndCostTests, InvoicePersistenceTests · a catalogue is changed after a sale and the bill is asserted unchanged

06Invoice numbers

Minted locally, gapless, and filed under the year a GST return actually covers.

RM/26-27/11358          # one till
RM/26-27/L1-11358       # with the lane segment
  • The year is the Indian financial year, 1 April to 31 March. A sequence that restarts on 1 January restarts in the middle of the year it will be filed under.
  • The number is taken inside the same transaction that writes the invoice, so a failed save returns it to the sequence rather than leaving a hole in a run that has to be unbroken.
  • The lane segment is what lets several tills number independently with nothing coordinating them. It can be dropped for a shop with exactly one till — and the setting says in terms what that would cost a shop that later buys a second.

Verified by InvoiceNumberFormatTests, InvoicePersistenceTests, CrashDurabilityTests · including both financial-year boundaries and the century wrap

07Closing the day

The Z-report leads with the cash figure, because the first thing anyone does with one is count the drawer against it.

Shift+F12 at the till, or pos close-day. It shows what it is about to close and asks twice, because a close cannot be undone. Closing takes a verified backup as part of the same operation.

  • A sale belongs to exactly one Z-report, ever. Invoices are stamped with the close that reported them rather than picked up by a time range, so closing twice is harmless and an old report stays reproducible.
  • The report prints its own three reconciliations — gross less discount, taxable plus tax, tenders less change — so a day that does not add up says so on its face.
  • Takings are split by cashier, which is what makes a drawer difference answerable rather than merely noted.
  • On a Tamil lane the report is in Tamil too: நாள் இறுதி அறிக்கை (Z).

Verified by DayCloseTests · including the report in both languages with identical figures

08Corrections

What can be undone, and what deliberately cannot.

Voiding shipped

Ctrl+Shift+V, or pos void-invoice. The bill stays in the books marked cancelled, its number stays used, the takings and the tax come out, loyalty points go back, and the drawer opens if there is cash to return.

Refused once the invoice has been on a Z-report. A closed day's figures have been filed, and changing a number somebody has acted on is not a correction. After that the instrument is a credit note — which this version does not do.

Reprinting shipped

Ctrl+P. The duplicate is marked ** REPRINT ** on its face, because an unmarked duplicate can be passed off as a second sale.

Verified by VoidSaleTests, VoidAndCashierFlowTests, ReprintAndCloseDayTests

09The dashboard

One self-contained HTML page. No scripts, no fonts, no network — it opens on a phone in the back room and can be sent to an accountant as a single file.

pos dashboard [--days 30] [--top 10] [--out dashboard.html]

It reads the books and writes nothing, on its own connection. SQLite in WAL mode lets it run while the till is billing, so a shopkeeper can look at four o'clock's figures at four o'clock.

SectionWhat it answers
TodayNet against gross, bill count, average basket, cash in drawer against digital
Takings by hourWhere the rush falls — and which hours are free for a delivery or a stock count
Daily trendThirty or ninety days with a seven-day mean over the top, because a grocery's week has a shape
Weekday × timeA slot that is quiet every week
What sellsRanked by takings, not by units — the two are rarely the same list
Department splitWhere the money came from, with unfiled items in one honest bucket
Margin × velocityStars, volume drivers, hidden gems, dead weight
How customers paidReconciling a drawer and a bank statement
GST by slabThe slab-wise figures a return is filed from
Given away, cancelledDiscounts, voided bills, points redeemed
CustomersKnown against walk-in, who came back, points earned against redeemed
The quadrant splits at the shop's own middle

Half the shop's items sell faster than the vertical line, half earn more than the horizontal one. A line drawn at a fixed 30% margin would say more about the line than about the shop, and every shop's normal is different.

Absence is carried through as absence

An item sold without a cost recorded is excluded from the margin picture, never plotted as keeping the whole of what it sells for — and the page reports how much of the takings it therefore cannot speak for. In the sample above: "covers 97% of the window's takings. Rs 5,355.00 came from 1 item with no cost price recorded." A chart that looked complete while describing a fraction of the trade is one somebody clears a shelf on.

Money is summed as whole paise

Amounts are stored as text to keep decimals exact, and SQLite has no decimal type. SUM(CAST(x AS REAL)) drifts across hundreds of thousands of rows — and the figure it drifts on is the one a GST return is filed from. Every aggregate multiplies by 100 and sums integers. A test adds two hundred amounts of ₹33.33 and demands exactly ₹6,666.00.

Verified by DashboardTests, CategoryAndCostTests · 33 checks

10Keeping the data

Every bill and every line stays for as long as the shop keeps the file. That is what makes them an audit trail — and it costs the counter nothing.

OperationFresh databaseTwo years of history
Saving an invoice3.59 ms4.21 ms
Barcode lookup0.028 ms0.029 ms
Dashboard, 30 days—259 ms

Measured against a 195 MB database holding 245,314 invoices and 981,769 lines. The partial index added for the dashboard is what keeps the aggregates proportional to the window rather than to the history.

What protects it

  • Backups — pos backup-db verifies the copy before calling it a backup, and does not block anyone billing. Closing the day takes one automatically and says whether it worked.
  • Integrity — pos check-db walks the whole file. The tests damage real files — a page of zeroes mid-file, a truncation, a wrecked header — and assert the check catches each.
  • Restore — pos restore-db checks the snapshot first and renames the database it replaces rather than deleting it.
  • Crash durability — a separate process is launched, allowed partway through a sale, and killed with no orderly shutdown. What survives is asserted: a committed invoice is still there, an uncommitted one left no trace, and the number an abandoned sale took went back to the sequence.

Verified by DatabaseBackupTests, DatabaseIntegrityTests, DatabaseRestoreTests, CrashDurabilityTests, OfflineResilienceTests

11Hardware

Signed off on real devices, with the figures recorded.

PeripheralResult
PrinterEpson TM-T82 over USB. Paper out, matching the preview, cut below the last line. 26.8 KB job, 42 ms to the spooler, ~1.2 s to paper.
Cash drawerRJ11 through the printer's passthrough port, fired on settlement
ScannerEAN-13 and internal SKUs, read straight onto the line
ScaleCAS stream on COM3 at 9600 8-N-1, settling to Stable with no dropped frames
TamilNirmala UI, crisp on thermal paper, no ? and no mojibake
Why the print was timed

A Tamil receipt is about 27 KB against 2 KB for the same bill in English, because the labels are drawn rather than typed. Over USB that is imperceptible. Over a printer on a 9600-baud serial line it would be roughly half a minute, and unusable at a counter. Nothing about the connection is visible from the software, so it had to be measured.

pos test-hardware shows what should come out before it prints, fires each peripheral, reports the job size and handover time, and asks the operator to confirm what physically happened — because no software can see paper leave a printer.

Verified by EscPosTests, ReceiptBuilderTests, ScaleProtocolTests, BarcodeTests, ScannerServiceTests, DrawerServiceTests · plus the bench sign-off sheet

12Shipping it

Two batch files, and an installer that cannot lie about its version.

build-installer        # tests, publish, and one setup.exe
run-acceptance         # drive the shipped build end to end

RetailPOS-Setup-1.1.0.exe — 98.6 MB, from a 348 MB payload. It installs per user and needs no admin rights; the two executables inside are self-contained, so the target machine needs nothing installed, not even the .NET runtime.

What the build refuses to do

  • Package a settings file pointing the printer at a file, or carrying a real store name or invoice prefix — a development rig cannot reach a shop by accident.
  • Package a template without its UTF-8 byte-order mark.
  • Build from an untagged commit or a dirty working tree. The version comes from the git tag, and what was passed in is read back off the built executable and checked.
  • Overwrite an existing settings.json on reinstall — a shop's identity and printer name are not the installer's to touch.
  • Delete the lane's database, settings or backups on uninstall. They are the shop's books.
Per user, not Program Files

A lane keeps its database and settings under the running user's LocalAppData. A per-machine install elevates, so where the person installing is not the person serving customers the settings would land in the wrong profile entirely — and the till would open on a lane with no settings while a perfectly good one sat in somebody else's folder. Installing per user makes that impossible.

Verified by installing it: fresh machine and configured lane, shortcuts, seeded settings, reinstall leaving the file byte-identical, and an uninstall with the books intact

13How it is tested

963 unit and integration tests, and 42 end-to-end checks that drive the shipped executables the way a person does.

The acceptance run photographs the till at each step and writes a single HTML report. Checks are reported in two sections, because they fail for opposite reasons: a positive failure means something is broken, and a negative failure means something that should have been refused went through — which on a till is the worse of the two.

It bills against a throwaway lane of its own and never touches a real one. That safety is checked rather than assumed: if the executable does not honour --data, the run stops before it reaches the till rather than putting test sales into a shop's books.

Two things worth knowing about the suite

  • Latency is measured as a median, not a mean. A mean over twenty iterations is one scheduling stall away from meaningless — and the median is the honest measure of whether a scan feels instant anyway.
  • Each test releases only its own database's pooled handles. A process-wide clear meant every test finishing yanked connections out from under every test still running, which produced failures that pointed at the wrong code entirely.

Full gate list in docs/TESTING_STRATEGY.md · every phase has a passing gate, hardware-in-the-loop included

14What it will not do

Known and deliberate, listed so nobody spends an afternoon looking.

AbsentWhy, and what to do instead
no Returns & refundsA proper GST credit note is its own piece of work. Voiding is not a refund — it cancels a sale that has not yet reached a Z-report, and stops working once the day is closed.
no Stock or inventoryThe catalogue holds prices, not quantities. No wastage tracking follows from this.
no Scale at the tillThe scale is tested by pos test-hardware but is not wired into the billing screen. Weights are keyed with F3.
no Opening floatCount it and write it down. The Z-report says what was taken; the float is added to that.
no Past Z-reports on screenEvery close is stored and reproducible, but nothing yet exposes an old one. The paper is the copy.
no Anything leaving the machineNot a gap — a design rule. The lane is entirely offline, and nothing leaves except what somebody copies off it.

Figures in this report are measured, not estimated: the latency table comes from a 195 MB database of simulated trading, the print timings from an Epson TM-T82 on a bench, and the screenshots from the running till and its real ESC/POS output.
